### Gradient Tool

`gradient`

Fills a selection or layer with a gradient you define by dragging: the click sets the first colour stop, the release the second.

The Gradient tool fills the current layer, or the selection when there is one, with a smooth blend between two or more colours. Where you click is where the first stop sits and where you release is where the second sits, so the drag sets the length and the angle of the gradient at once, and the gradient clamps to its ends beyond the drag rather than fading to transparent - which is why a short drag fills everything. The bar runs from a tool-preset picker, past the Tool Mode dropdown, to the gradient swatch and then through the five gradient types, the Dither and Reverse checkboxes and a Method dropdown, and every one of those controls belongs to the tool itself rather than to a brush. A blend Mode, an Opacity and a Transparency checkbox are also part of the Gradient tool, but only on the older destructive Classic gradient: on the live tool they are layer properties in the Layers panel instead. From 24.5 the bar also offers that Tool Mode dropdown, which picks between the two, and the live gradient can be corrected after the fact by dragging its handles on the canvas.

**Options bar**

| Control                    | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | In this app                                                          |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tool Preset Picker         | The button at the left end of the bar, before everything else, which opens the drop-down of saved tool presets for the Gradient tool. Photoshop ships one - a "Circular Rainbow" - and it is the control every tool carries for recalling a saved bar configuration, so it is the bar's first stop rather than a Gradient-specific setting.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `missing`                                                            |
| Tool Mode                  | The dropdown immediately to the right of the Tool Preset picker, picking between "Gradient" and "Classic gradient". It exists only in 24.5 and later, and it is not cosmetic: the choice changes which options follow it, since Mode, Opacity and Transparency belong to the Classic one alone. The classic tool is destructive and must be reapplied after Dither or Reverse changes; the live one writes an editable gradient adjustment layer instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                                            |
| Gradient preset picker     | The gradient swatch just to the right of the Tool Mode dropdown. Clicking it opens the Gradient Editor, where the stops, their locations, their colours, their opacity stops and their midpoints are edited and the preset saved; its dropdown arrow opens the presets library instead. It is two controls in one swatch, and the two do different things. On the live tool the Gradient Editor cannot be opened this way at all - the swatch is read-only there, and a live gradient is edited from its adjustment layer instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                | `missing`                                                            |
| Gradient Type              | Five buttons: Linear, a straight ramp from the start point to the end point; Radial, a circle from the start point at its centre to the end point at its outer edge; Angle, a sweep in the direction the drag points; Reflected, a linear ramp mirrored about the start point; and Diamond, a rhombus radiating from it. Linear is the default, and Angle, Reflected and Diamond are the three most often left off a smaller implementation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Gradient/Gradient.tsx:13`  |
| Mode                       | The blend mode the gradient is composited with, Normal by default, which is how a gradient is used to tint or to knock back whatever is beneath it rather than to replace it. It is a control of the Classic gradient only: on the live (default) Gradient tool there is no Mode in the bar at all, because the gradient is written as an adjustment layer and the blend mode is a property of that layer in the Layers panel instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `missing`                                                            |
| Opacity                    | The opacity of the whole gradient, 0-100% and 100% by default. It scales the fill and is not a third stop: the gradient keeps its own alpha ramp, and this multiplies it. It is a control of the Classic gradient only - the teachucomp walkthrough is explicit that the Mode and Opacity drop-downs "do not appear in the Options bar Control panel if using the new Gradient Tool, as it applies its gradient adjustment in a separate adjustment layer", and on the live tool opacity is the adjustment layer's own property. So this row describes a control that is not on the 27.x bar for the default tool, and the app's status is partial because it renders a slider in a place Photoshop has moved the setting out of. | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Gradient/Gradient.tsx:129` |
| Dither                     | It adds noise at the boundaries of each colour in the interpolation so transitions appear smoother, which is what stops an 8-bit ramp from showing visible banding. On a live gradient the setting is live, so ticking it updates the existing gradient immediately; on the Classic tool it has to be reapplied. No Adobe page states a default for it, and a third-party walkthrough is the only one that calls it one, describing Dither-on and Perceptual as "both the default settings".                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `missing`                                                            |
| Transparency               | Enables the gradient pattern transparency. It is not available on the new Gradient tool at all - the checkbox belongs to the Classic gradient only - and with it off the opacity stops in the gradient are ignored.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `missing`                                                            |
| Reverse                    | Swaps the gradient ends, so the colour that was at the first stop moves to the second. As with Dither it is live on a live gradient and requires reapplying the gradient on the Classic tool, and as with Dither no page I opened states a default for it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | `missing`                                                            |
| Method                     | The interpolation method: Perceptual, which is the default and interpolates in the OKLab colour space so the ramp looks natural to the eye; Linear, which interpolates in linear colour space; and Classic, the interpolation Photoshop used for decades, kept for backwards compatibility. Perceptual became the default in 23.0, so gradients made in 22.x or earlier render differently in 23.0 and later unless this is set back to Classic.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | `missing`                                                            |
| On-canvas gradient handles | Not an options-bar control but the tool defining editing surface, and the load-bearing one. After the drag, two round handles mark the gradient ends and a small diamond between them sets the midpoint, all draggable straight on the canvas. Dragging a handle re-aims the gradient and changes its length; dragging the line itself - avoiding the dots and the diamond - moves the whole gradient rather than one end of it, and no modifier is involved. Photoshop added these on-canvas controls together with an automatic live preview in 24.5.                                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                                            |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the drag to multiples of 45 degrees, so a linear gradient lands on a square angle. NOT IMPLEMENTED in this app — gradient.ts and GradientToolArea.tsx have no Shift handling for angle constraint.

**Shortcuts**

- `G` — Reaches the Gradient tool, but only on the second press: a plain G selects the Paint Bucket, and it is Shift+G that cycles the pair. The Gradient tile declares no shortcut letter of its own, while the Paint Bucket's declares G.
- `Delete` — In Photoshop, removes the stop under the pointer from the on-canvas gradient line. The app has no editable on-canvas gradient handles or stops, so this binding is not implemented here.

**In this app:** `partial` — The fill itself is right: the drag sets both endpoints, the projection clamps to the ends rather than fading to transparent, and a linear ramp puts the exact mean of the two stops at the midpoint of the axis. Everything around it is thinner than the bar. The bar has four controls where Photoshop's bar has eleven, and it does not even start where Photoshop's does: the Tool Preset picker is the control at the left end of the Photoshop bar and this bar opens with `Type` instead, so there is no saved-preset recall at all. Gradient Type offers only Linear and Radial - Angle, Reflected and Diamond have no representation in a fixed from/to pair. The Radial is also a different fill: the app's holds its end colour past the circle through the second stop, and no page I opened states that Photoshop mirrors there, so that difference is recorded as a structural consequence of the fixed `from`/`to` args rather than as a Photoshop behaviour. Dither, Reverse and the Method dropdown are all missing, and Method is the most consequential omission of the three: the app interpolates the two stops as plain per-channel RGB, which is closest to the Classic behaviour that Photoshop stopped defaulting to in 23.0, so every gradient this editor paints is one Method dropdown away from a different ramp. The Tool Mode dropdown is missing too, so there is no live/classic choice at all - the app is permanently the destructive one, and even a Dither checkbox would have had to be reapplied by hand. Transparency is absent, which happens to match the modern tool rather than the Classic one, but for the wrong reason: there is no alpha ramp at all. The Opacity slider is the one control the app carries that Photoshop has taken off the live tool's bar entirely - on the Classic gradient it is a bar dropdown, and on the live one it is the adjustment layer's own property in the Layers panel - so the app shows a control Photoshop moved, which is why that row is `partial` and not `present`. The preset picker and the Gradient Editor are gone, so there are no multi-stop gradients, no per-stop opacity or position, no midpoints, and no gradient styles. The two stops are two colour inputs in the bar rather than a picker, and they are the tool's only gradient state - there is no Foreground-to-Background preset and nothing to reset to. The load-bearing gap is the on-canvas handles: the tool area accepts the overlay context and never draws to it, and from/to are written only by the drag, so once the fill is committed its geometry cannot be changed at all without painting a second gradient over it. Photoshop's live-preview gradient, added in 24.5, is not a refinement of that - it is the difference between a fill and an editable object. Nothing is bound to Shift, so a drag is never constrained to a square angle. The two preset keys are bound nowhere in the app at all: `,` and `.` are on no keyboard handler, and `[` and `]` are registered but as the shared tip-size nudge, which is gated to the tools that carry a tip-size field and the Gradient is not one of them, so both are dead while this tool is active. The only `Delete` bindings belong to the two lasso tool areas, so no key removes a gradient stop. The bar's four controls are not the ones Photoshop sequences, so a user arriving from Photoshop finds neither the Order nor the Method. The verdict is `partial` and not `placeholder` because the fill does reach the document as a real raster with a real history entry; what it commits is not what Photoshop's tool commits, which is a narrower gradient with no editable object left behind.

### Blur Tool

`blur`

Paints blur under the brush, softening hard edges and reducing detail wherever you drag; the effect builds up pass by pass.

The Blur tool reduces local contrast and smooths detail in the areas you paint it over, so one pass is subtle and repeated passes are not. It shares a Tools-panel slot, options bar and tip with Sharpen and Smudge: Adobe documents a brush preset with Size/Hardness, Strength and Sample All Layers. Blur-specific control remains unconfirmed for a separate Mode field, so this description does not infer one from global blend-mode lists. It is a different thing from Filter > Blur and from the Blur Gallery, which run a Gaussian, Box, Lens, Motion, Radial, Smart, Surface or Tilt-Shift, Iris or Field blur over a whole selection or layer in one command with no brush and no per-stroke build-up.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | In this app |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the blur is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. Photoshop exposes the whole preset library here; Size and Hardness are the preset's two live parameters, and a soft tip is what lets a stroke blend into its surroundings instead of standing out against them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `missing`   |
| Strength            | The percentage of the blurred result blended in per pass, 1-100% and 50% by default. It is the per-stroke build-up rate, not a radius: at 100% one pass is the full blur, and at a low value the same stroke has to be repeated to get there. Adobe and the CS-era documentation both describe 10-30% as the subtle setting and 50% or more as strong. The 1% floor is not Adobe's own statement - no Adobe page gives the range either way - but the CS2 Bible states it directly ("1 percent being the minimum and 100 percent being the maximum"), and a 2009 report on the tool repeats that the range is 1-100%. | `missing`   |
| Sample All Layers   | Off by default. With it on, the blur samples the composite of every visible layer, so painting on a blank layer above the stack produces a separable, opacity-adjustable result; with it off the tool reads only the active layer. The blur is written into whichever layer is active either way.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `missing`   |

**Shortcuts**

- `R` — Photoshop assigns R to the Blur/Sharpen/Smudge family. THIS APP DIVERGES: R selects Rotate View; it has no Shift+R cycle for this family.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app's blur is a whole-layer FILTER, not a paint tool, and the two are not the same thing. Its options bar is a single Blur Radius slider plus an Undo Blur button; there is no brush, no Size, no Hardness, no Mode, no Strength and no Sample All Layers, because the bar's only argument is a radius in pixels that the processor hands straight to the canvas blur filter. There is no gesture surface at all: `Main`'s tool-area dispatch has no `blur` branch, so the canvas area for blur falls through to `DummyToolArea`, the inert `display: none` surface every unrouted tool gets. That is a different component from the Sharpen's: the Sharpen mounts a `SharpenToolArea` of its own, which also renders `display: none` and is documented as the deliberate absence of a gesture. Two components with the same rendering, not one. So nothing can be painted, and the whole active layer is previewed as soon as the slider moves: the bar routes through `tempUpdateLayer`, which publishes a preview layer and no history entry, and the entry is written later by the dirty-tool commit on tool switch, on export or in `mergeAllLayers`. That makes it the closest thing this editor has to Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur - a true Gaussian, with the canvas blur filter as its kernel - wearing Photoshop's Blur tool's name. The verdict is `partial` and not `placeholder` for one specific reason, and it is the same reason the Sharpen's is: the tool does reach the document. It commits a real blurred raster with a real history entry, and `placeholder` is defined as committing nothing. What it commits is simply not what Photoshop's tool commits, which is what `partial` is for. Every one of the four controls above is therefore absent rather than incomplete. `Flow` is not one of them: no page I opened puts it on the Blur bar, so it is omitted from the table as unsourced rather than recorded as a gap - and the app could not have rendered it in any case, having no per-dab and per-stroke opacity pair to express one with, so the omission costs no fidelity claim.

### Sharpen Tool

`sharpen`

Paints extra edge contrast where you drag, so a soft area reads sharper without sharpening the rest of the image at all.

The Sharpen tool increases local contrast at edges, and therefore the apparent sharpness, only in the areas you brush. It shares one options bar and one tip with the Blur and Smudge tools, and what separates it from the Blur is the direction of the local change: the Blur smooths, the Sharpen exaggerates the difference between neighbouring pixels over a wider radius, with a falloff that behaves like an unsharp mask rather than a flat average. Its bar carries a brush preset, a Mode, a Strength percentage, Sample All Layers and Protect Detail. It is not the Filter > Sharpen family: those are one-shot commands with no brush and no per-stroke build-up, and Sharpen More in particular is simply the Sharpen filter with a larger fixed amount and no controls of its own.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | In this app |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the sharpening is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A small hard tip over one edge and a large soft tip over a whole face are two different jobs, and the tool has no other way to express that choice.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `missing`   |
| Mode                | The blend mode the sharpened result is composited with as you brush. Adobe’s October 2026 desktop guide lists this control, but neither page enumerates Sharpen’s tool-specific blend-mode set. Adobe’s blending-mode page lists 11 modes for 32-bit images; its 32-bpc HDR support page lists 15 for 32-bpc HDR images. Since 32-bpc HDR is a 32-bit scope, the lists overlap, and Adobe does not reconcile their different counts. The HDR page includes Sharpen among supported tools.                        | `missing`   |
| Strength            | How much sharpening each pass contributes, 1-100% and 50% by default. It is a per-stroke build-up rate on a filtered copy of the pixels under the brush, not a kernel radius; the effect accumulates with repeated passes over the same place, and at 10-20% it is subtle where at 50% or more it degrades quickly. No Adobe page gives the range either way; the CS2 Bible states the floor directly ("1 percent being the minimum and 100 percent being the maximum") for the Blur and Sharpen Strength alike. | `missing`   |
| Protect Detail      | On by default, and on the current desktop bar rather than an Elements leftover. Adobe enumerates it there between Strength and Sample All Layers as "Select Protect Detail to minimize pixelation and maintain image quality" - the sharpening is what produces the pixelation and this is the checkbox that keeps it from doing so. The wording is the same one Adobe used for the Sharpen tool in Photoshop Elements, where it "ensures minimized pixelated artifacts while enhancing and sharpening".         | `missing`   |
| Sample All Layers   | Off by default. With it on, the tool sharpens using the composite of every visible layer, so on a blank layer above the stack the sharpening is a separable, opacity-adjustable layer rather than a destructive change to the pixels underneath.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | `missing`   |

**Shortcuts**

- `R` — Photoshop assigns R to the Blur/Sharpen/Smudge family. THIS APP DIVERGES: R selects Rotate View; it has no Shift+R cycle for this family.

**In this app:** `partial` — What the app ships under this name is the Filter > Sharpen > Unsharp Mask filter, not the tool. The options bar is Amount (0-500%, 50% by default) and Radius (0-100 px, 1 px by default) - the Unsharp Mask's own control names, not the tool's - and there is no brush, no Strength, no Mode, no Sample All Layers and no Protect Detail. The Radius is the sharper divergence of the two, because Photoshop's tool has no radius control at all: the bar Adobe enumerates runs brush Size and Hardness, Strength, Protect Detail, Sample All Layers, and a write-up on the CS5 rebuild is explicit that 'the tool has no radius control, so it's really just for screen sharpening'. A slider the tool does not have is a control rendered in a place Photoshop has nothing, which is the same defect the Gradient's Opacity slider is filed under. There is no gesture either: the Sharpen's canvas area renders display:none by design, so nothing can be brushed. The layer is previewed when a slider moves rather than committed by it: the bar routes through `tempUpdateLayer`, which publishes a preview layer and no history entry, and the entry is written later by the dirty-tool commit on tool switch, on export or in `mergeAllLayers`. As on the Blur, the verdict is `partial` and not `placeholder` because the tool does reach the document: it commits a real convolved raster with a real history entry, and `placeholder` is defined as committing nothing. The kernel is a two-pass separable BOX blur subtracted from the source, which is an unsharp mask over a box kernel rather than over Photoshop's Gaussian; the file says so. That matters more for this tool than for the filter, because the addendum's own account of the three focus tools is that they are distinguished precisely by kernel behaviour - the Blur smooths, the Sharpen uses a wider radius with unsharp-like falloff rather than a box blur. The kernel class is not the gap here, because the app does have the box kernel and says so in caps. What is missing is Photoshop's Gaussian: a real unsharp mask subtracts a Gaussian-blurred copy, whose response decays smoothly away from an edge, while a box window responds flatly across its whole width and stops dead at the edge. At small radii the two are nearly interchangeable; at a wide one the app's Sharpen hardens a band of the full window width with a step at its boundary, where Photoshop tapers. So the Blur and the Sharpen here differ in radius and in magnitude, not in the shape of the kernel's response - which is exactly the distinction the addendum says separates them, and the app does not reproduce it. The one genuine strength here is over the pixels underneath: the blur runs on premultiplied colour with alpha unsharp-masked on its own scale, so a transparent hole does not bleed a ring into the opaque side - a halo Photoshop's own USM does not go out of its way to avoid either.

### Smudge Tool

`smudge`

Drags the pixels under the brush along the stroke, picking up colour where the stroke begins and pushing it where you pull.

The Smudge tool simulates a finger through wet paint: it picks up the colour where the stroke starts and pushes it in the direction you drag, blending what it carries into what it passes over. It is the only one of the three focus tools that transports rather than transforms, which is why it is the only one that needs Sample All Layers, the only one with Finger Painting, and the only one where sampling the wrong pixels shows up as a visible smear. Alongside the brush preset and Mode the bar has a Strength percentage - where 100% is described as effectively infinite, carrying one colour the whole length of the drag - plus Finger Painting, which starts each stroke with the foreground colour instead of the colour under the pointer.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | In this app                                                      |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the smudge is carried with, carrying its Size and Hardness. The smudge is the size of the fingertip, so the preset is a statement about scale rather than about texture.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Smudge/Smudge.tsx:138` |
| Mode                | The blend mode the carried colour is composited with; Adobe's own page for this tool puts "blend mode options" on the bar without naming a default, and Normal is the one every painting tool starts on. Darken and Lighten are the useful ones here: they smear only the pixels that are darker or lighter than the colour the stroke started on, which is how a smudge is used to push a background out from behind a subject.                                                                                                                                                                               | `missing`                                                        |
| Strength            | The percentage of the carried colour blended per dab, 1-100% and 50% by default. A Strength of 100% is described as equivalent to infinity: it carries the colour sampled at the start of the drag all the way to the release, at which point the smudge is effectively painting. Below 100% the carried colour fades and picks up the new colour under the brush as it goes. No Adobe page gives the range either way; the CS2 Bible covers the Smudge Strength in the same paragraph as the Blur and Sharpen one and gives the same floor ("1 percent being the minimum and 100 percent being the maximum"). | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Smudge/Smudge.tsx:168` |
| Finger Painting     | Off by default, and called "dipping" in older versions of Photoshop. With it on, the stroke first applies a drop of the foreground colour and blends it into the image, then smudges that through as if a finger had been dipped in paint; the Strength setting then specifies how much foreground colour is applied, so at 100% the Smudge becomes the Brush. With it off, the colour under the pointer at the start of the stroke is used instead.                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                                        |
| Sample All Layers   | Off by default, and called "Use All Layers" before CS2. With it on, the tool grabs colour from every visible layer and smudges it into the current layer. The layers underneath are not modified either way, which is what makes the recommended workflow - a new empty layer with the box ticked - non-destructive.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                                        |

**Shortcuts**

- `R` — The current desktop Smudge guide says R cycles through retouching tools; the 2023 guide labels Smudge with R; a 2019 Photoshop reference lists R for Rotate View. Adobe directs users to the Keyboard Shortcuts and Menus dialog to inspect the active binding. THIS APP binds R to Rotate View and has no Shift+R cycle for this family.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — This is the closest match in the family. The processor reads each covered pixel from the untouched source raster at the texel one dab-behind along the drag, never from the buffer it is writing, so colour travels exactly one segment per dab instead of compounding into a single streak; the falloff is the shared brush engine's tipAlphaAt, so the smudge's soft edge is the same edge the Brush, Eraser, Dodge, Burn and Clone Stamp stamp. Strength is a real per-dab coverage seeded at 50% as in Photoshop, and it is `partial` rather than `present` for one narrow reason: the bar lets the slider reach 0, where `SMUDGE_STRENGTH_MIN` is 0 and the module says so in caps, while every source that states a floor for this Strength puts it at 1%. The transport semantics are right, and the app matches Photoshop's layering rule without being told to: the stroke edits the active layer, which is exactly what Sample All Layers does not change. Three controls are missing rather than wrong. Mode has nowhere to live because no control anywhere in the app edits a layer's blend mode: `Layer.blendMode` is a data field the paint tool's own Mode select writes and the PSD importer sets, and a grep for `blendMode` across `src/components/` finds only that select - the Layers panel has no blend-mode control at all. Finger Painting needs an args field of its own before it can be a control, and it is a per-dab source selection rather than a setting on the same axis as the other three. Sample All Layers would need the composite, and the processor is handed one layer's bitmap. The Brush Preset Picker is partial rather than absent because this editor has one tip shape and no presets, though Size and Hardness - the preset's two live parameters - are both there. Alt is not bound to Finger Painting. There is no build-up while the button is held: the shared stroke hook appends a point to the drag on a pointer move and there is no timer and no dwell accumulation anywhere in it, so holding the brush still deposits nothing, and one stroke is one undo entry. That is the same absence this file calls the tool's defining interaction on the Dodge and the Burn, and it is why this tool is filed `partial` on the same bar rather than `implemented` - not because the drag misbehaves, which it does not, but because the interaction the tool exists for is not there.

### Dodge Tool

`dodge` · **O**

Lightens the tonal range you choose as you paint, the way holding back paper under a finger brightens a print.

The Dodge tool comes from the darkroom: a printer holds light back under a finger to lighten that part of the print, and this is the digital version. Dragging it lightens the pixels it passes over, and it keeps doing so for as long as the button is held, so the effect is built by dwelling rather than by painting more. It is a tone operation gated by a tonal range, which is what separates it from the Sponge tool in the same flyout - the Sponge is a chroma operation with a Saturate/Desaturate mode and neither a Range nor an Exposure. Exposure is the only intensity control on the bar: there is no Opacity and no Flow, unlike the paint tools. The bar also offers Airbrush, which makes the build-up automatic while the brush rests, and Protect Tones, which is on by default and keeps the lightening from shifting hue or clipping the ends of the range.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | In this app                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the dodge is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A large soft tip with a low Exposure is how a dodge is built gradually; a small hard one is how a catchlight is placed.                                                                                                                                 | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:156` |
| Range               | Which tonal range the stroke is allowed to touch: Shadows, Midtones or Highlights, with Midtones as the default. Choosing the range is what makes the same tool usable on a face without taking the specular highlights with it, and it is why the Dodge and Burn are tone operations while the Sponge beside them is not. | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:126` |
| Exposure            | How strongly each pass lightens, as a percentage, 0-100% with 50% as the default, and the only intensity control on the bar. A low value with repeated passes is the intended workflow; a high one in a single pass is how a dodge turns into a blown highlight.                                                           | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:139` |
| Protect Tones       | On by default. A boolean that changes which pixels the stroke will touch: it helps maintain colour and prevents clipping in the highlights and shadows, which is the same work Adobe's older bar called Protect Skin Tone.                                                                                                 | `missing`                                                      |
| Airbrush            | Off by default. With it on, the effect keeps building on its own wherever the brush rests, without needing a new stroke - the automatic version of what holding the button still otherwise does, and the reason the tool is a "toning tool" that can build up "on the fly".                                                | `missing`                                                      |

**Shortcuts**

- `O` — Selects the Dodge tool; the letter is shared with the Burn and Sponge tools in the same flyout.
- `Shift+O` — Cycles through the tools that share the O shortcut, which reaches the Burn tool without leaving the canvas.
- `0–9` — In Photoshop, number keys 0–9 set Exposure: 0 = 100%, 1 = 10%, and two quick digits set an exact percentage. With Airbrush enabled, use Shift+number to set Opacity. This app does not implement Dodge Exposure digit shortcuts.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — Range and Exposure are both real and both wired: Range writes a field the processor reads, and Exposure drives a per-pixel amount rather than a display-only value, with the band's power driven by the exposure so a high value narrows the band instead of dragging a hard edge across the picture. The band itself is a quadratic falloff in Rec.709 luma of the encoded sRGB the editor stores, split at a flat luma 128. That is a defensible reading of what the tool does - Photoshop also scales stored channel values towards 255 - but it is a single hard split against a real tonal scale, and the three Photoshop bands are not equal halves of the range. The bar also matches Photoshop in a negative that is easy to get wrong: there is no Opacity and no Flow, only Exposure, which is why `DodgeBurnToolArgs` has no opacity or spacing field and takes both from the shared engine's defaults. Three controls are missing. There is no `Mode` control on the Dodge or Burn bar to be missing: the blend mode is fixed, and Peachpit's account of the tools is that they 'are effectively operating with the Color Burn and Color Dodge blending modes', which is why they shift colour and why Protect Tones has to be there to hold the colour back. Protect Tones is a real omission and the component says so: there is no field for it, so a checkbox would read as on while doing nothing. Airbrush is missing for the same reason. The Brush Preset Picker is partial rather than absent because Size and Hardness, the preset's two live parameters, are both present and clamped to 1-500 px and 0-100%. The largest behavioural gap is not a control: there is NO BUILD-UP. Each stroke commits once, at the slider's full Exposure value in a single pass, because a one-shot commit has to be a pure function of its args, which is also what makes the registry's replay reproduce it exactly. Holding the button still does nothing, so the tool's defining interaction is absent - and Airbrush, which exists precisely to make that build-up automatic when you cannot hold still, is missing for the same reason. Dodge and Burn deliberately share one options component, so a change to this control set cannot land on one tool and miss the other. This app does not implement Exposure digit shortcuts for Dodge or Burn.

### Burn Tool

`burn`

Darkens the tonal range you choose as you paint, the way letting more light onto a print deepens its shadows.

The Burn tool is the Dodge tool measured from the other end: instead of holding light back, you let more of it onto the print, which deepens that part of the image. Dragging darkens the pixels it passes over, and it keeps darkening for as long as the button is held. Range confines the work to Shadows, Midtones or Highlights, and Exposure - the bar's only intensity control, with no Opacity and no Flow - sets how hard each pass works. Airbrush makes the build-up automatic while the brush rests, and Protect Tones is on by default and keeps the darkening from raising saturation or clipping the shadows and highlights.

**Options bar**

| Control             | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | In this app                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker | The tip the burn is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A large soft tip with a low Exposure builds a burn gradually; a small hard one places a precise one.                                                                                               | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:156` |
| Range               | Which tonal range the stroke is allowed to touch: Shadows, Midtones or Highlights, with Midtones as the default. Restricting a burn to the shadows is what keeps it from muddying the midtones it was not aimed at.                                                  | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:126` |
| Exposure            | How strongly each pass darkens, as a percentage, 0-100% with 50% as the default, and the only intensity control on the bar. Low values with repeated passes are the intended workflow; a high one in a single pass closes the shadows up.                            | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Tonal/Tonal.tsx:139` |
| Protect Tones       | On by default. A boolean that changes which pixels the stroke will touch: without it a burn raises the saturation of what it darkens as well as darkening it, and it can clip the ends of the range. This is the control Adobe's older bar called Protect Skin Tone. | `missing`                                                      |
| Airbrush            | Off by default. With it on, the darkening keeps building wherever the brush rests, without needing a new stroke.                                                                                                                                                     | `missing`                                                      |

**Shortcuts**

- `0–9` — In Photoshop, number keys 0–9 set Exposure: 0 = 100%, 1 = 10%, and two quick digits set an exact percentage. With Airbrush enabled, use Shift+number to set Opacity. This app does not implement Burn Exposure digit shortcuts.
- `Shift+O` — Cycles from the Dodge tool to the Burn tool, which share the O shortcut; press it again to reach the Sponge tool.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — The same processor as the Dodge, with the endpoint swapped: the burn's rule is c' = c - c * amount against the dodge's c' = c + (255 - c) * amount, and the module is explicit that burn is not the inverse of dodge. Range and Exposure are both wired to real per-pixel work through the same band function, and the band is a quadratic falloff in Rec.709 luma of the encoded sRGB the editor stores - a defensible reading, since Photoshop also scales stored channel values towards 0, but a single hard split at luma 128 where the three real tonal bands are not equal halves of the range. Protect Tones and Airbrush are both missing for the same reason as on the Dodge: `DodgeBurnToolArgs` has no field to hold them, and a control that renders a value the processor never reads is the failure this bar is written against. As on the Dodge there is no `Mode` control to miss, because the blend mode is fixed in Photoshop rather than selectable. The Brush Preset Picker is partial because Size and Hardness are present. The defining gap is again the absence of build-up while the button is held - one stroke, one commit, at the slider's full Exposure value in a single pass - which is a deliberate choice to keep the commit a pure function of its args so the registry replays it exactly, and which costs the tool the behaviour it exists for. This tool and the Dodge share one options component by design, so the control set cannot drift between them. This app does not implement Exposure digit shortcuts for Dodge or Burn.

### Sponge Tool

`sponge`

Raises or lowers the colour saturation under the brush, so a flat area gains colour or a loud one loses it, and the lightness underneath is untouched.

The Sponge tool subtly changes the colour saturation of an area. Saturate intensifies the colour's saturation and Desaturate dilutes it, and the tool reaches no further than that: it is the one brush in the toning flyout that acts on chroma rather than on tone, which is what separates it from the Dodge and the Burn beside it, and neither a Range nor an Exposure appears on its bar because neither means anything to a chroma operation. Flow is the bar's only intensity control, and where the Dodge and the Burn have neither Opacity nor Flow the Sponge has Flow and no Opacity. A generic Photoshop shortcut reference assigns Shift+number to Flow, but the current Sponge-specific guide does not confirm a numeric binding; treat that generic evidence cautiously, especially for Airbrush. Dragging compounds: the effect builds up pass by pass and keeps building for as long as the button is held, which is why retouching with it is done at a low Flow with repeated passes. Adobe documents one more thing about it that belongs here rather than in the option table, because it is a rule rather than a control: when an image is in Grayscale mode the tool increases or decreases contrast by moving grey levels away from or toward the middle grey. Vibrance, the checkbox that sits beside Flow, is what keeps the Saturate direction from pushing an already-bright colour off the end of its range; it arrived with the CS4 rework of all three toning tools, which is the same release that gave the Dodge and the Burn Protect Tones.

**Options bar**

| Control               | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | In this app                                                      |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brush Preset Picker   | The tip the sponge is painted with, carrying its Size and Hardness. A large soft tip at a low Flow is how a whole area is evened out; a small hard one is how one stubborn patch is treated.                                                                                                                                                   | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:172` |
| Mode                  | Saturate or Desaturate, and nothing else: Adobe names exactly the two, as 'Saturate: Intensifies the color's saturation' and 'Desaturate: Dilutes the color's saturation'. Which one is the default is not something Adobe states anywhere, so the app's own seeded value is recorded as a choice rather than as an Adobe fact.                | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:133` |
| Flow                  | The rate at which the saturation changes, as a percentage, 1-100%, and the bar's only intensity control. Adobe describes it only as setting 'the rate of saturation change' and states neither a default nor a range; the 1% floor and the 50% seed are the CS2 Bible's and a third-party walkthrough's, not Adobe's.                          | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:146` |
| Vibrance              | Adobe's only documented description of it is 'Select the Vibrance option to minimize clipping for fully saturated or desaturated colors', so it is a gamut guard rather than a second intensity control: with it on the stroke cannot push a channel off the end of its range. Whether Adobe ships it checked is not stated on any page found. | `present` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Sponge/Sponge.tsx:163` |
| Airbrush              | Off by default. With it on, the saturation keeps building wherever the brush rests without needing a new stroke. It is listed in community descriptions of the bar rather than in Adobe own enumeration of it.                                                                                                                                 | `missing`                                                        |
| Use Pressure for Size | A pressure-tablet toggle that sizes the tip by how hard the stylus is pressed. No tool in this app reads tablet pressure, so the control would have nothing behind it.                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                                        |

**Shortcuts**

- `Shift+0–9` — The 2019 generic painting/editing shortcut reference says Shift+number sets Flow. This is historical generic evidence rather than a current Sponge-specific confirmation; for Airbrush, it does not establish whether that exception applies to the Sponge.
- `O` — Selects the Dodge tool. Adobe lists the Dodge, the Burn and the Sponge as three rows with the same letter rather than one row, which puts the Dodge first; the Sponge is reached by cycling.
- `Shift+O` — Cycles from the Dodge tool to the Burn tool and on to the Sponge, which share the O shortcut.
- `Shift+Alt+D` — Sets the tool to Desaturate while the Sponge is active. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+D on macOS.
- `Shift+Alt+S` — Sets the tool to Saturate while the Sponge is active - and is Shadows on the Dodge and the Burn, on the same page of the same Adobe table, so the two tools share one key and Photoshop resolves it by which tool is selected. Photoshop prints it Shift+Option+S on macOS.
- `[` — Decreases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.
- `]` — Increases the brush tip size by one pixel, and repeats as a scrub while the key is held.

**In this app:** `partial` — This is filed partial on two independent grounds, and both are stated here rather than left for the next reader to infer. The first is the one the Dodge, the Burn and the Smudge already carry: there is no build-up. Photoshop's Sponge compounds for as long as the button is held and every tutorial retouches it at a low Flow with repeated passes, while this app commits once per stroke, on release, at the Flow value in full. That is what keeps the commit a pure function of its args, which is in turn what lets the registry's raster replay reproduce it exactly, and the cost is the tool's defining interaction - the same cost `docs/TOOLS-TOO-HARD.md` records for the other two toning tools. Flow therefore means 'the whole effect of one pass' here rather than Photoshop's 'the strength of one dab', and the two are only the same number at Flow 100. The second is the Vibrance checkbox: it is a control welded to one of its two states. It caps the chroma scale at the pixel's own gamut boundary, which is the strictest reading of Adobe's 'minimize clipping', and that cap can only ever bind in the Saturate direction - Desaturate moves every channel toward the pixel's own luma, so its result is the convex combination of two in-range values and provably cannot leave the range, which makes the checkbox do nothing in that mode. Airbrush and Use Pressure for Size are missing for the reasons given in the option table: the first is the build-up above and the second is a tablet this app does not read. Protect Texture and Tolerance are deliberately absent from this record's option table rather than filed as missing: no source puts Protect Texture on the Sponge's own bar (it is a Brush-panel checkbox) and none puts Tolerance on it at all - it belongs to the Magic Wand and the Color Replacement. Adobe's bare digit keys step Flow on this tool, because the Sponge has a Flow and no Opacity, and the app's Opacity table has no Sponge entry, so 0 and 1 do nothing here; that is recorded rather than listed, since the shortcut table describes Photoshop. Adobe's Grayscale-mode rule is also not implemented, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight: the rule pivots grey levels about mid-grey in a document MODE this app does not have, and on an RGB pixel with no chroma the chroma scale is already an exact no-op, so adding the pivot would make the tool behave the way Photoshop behaves in a mode that cannot be reached. Grayscale PSDs are expanded to RGB on import and the source mode is not retained, so that no-op reasoning does not settle the Photoshop-specific behavior for imported grayscale pixels; the current tool cannot distinguish those from ordinary achromatic RGB. Two seeded values are choices Adobe declines to document rather than divergences from it, and both are recorded in full at `SPONGE_MODE_DEFAULT` and `SPONGE_FLOW_DEFAULT`: no Adobe page states which Mode the bar opens on, and no Adobe page states a Flow default. The Mode seeds at Desaturate because it is the non-destructive direction - a saturated stroke that clips a channel cannot be painted back - and Flow at the midpoint of the range every other percentage control in this app uses. The pixel arithmetic is a chroma scale about a Rec.709 luma of the ENCODED sRGB the editor stores, in the same space and for the same stated reason as the Dodge and the Burn, rather than in a colour space Adobe names and this repo does not have; Adobe publishes no per-pixel specification for this tool, and the one community implementation that states its rule says the same thing. One deliberate departure from `computeLuma`: the pivot reads the stored channels and does not fold alpha in the way the shared helper does, because folding alpha composites a partly transparent pixel toward white and would drag its hue with it - the opposite of what a chroma tool should do to a cut-out edge. A fully transparent pixel is left alone outright. The stroke coverage field is the shared one, extracted out of `dodgeBurn.ts` into `src/util/stroke-coverage.ts` rather than written a second time, and dabs are unioned rather than summed so a replay cannot compound. The 2026 Sponge guide documents Flow but no numeric binding; a 2019 generic painting/editing reference assigns Flow to Shift+number. No Shift+number handler sets Flow in this app.

## Shapes

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/shape.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/shape.notes.md).

### Rectangle Tool

`rectangle` · **U**

Drag-defined rectangle or square with an optional corner radius, drawn as a shape layer, path, or filled pixels.

The Rectangle tool draws a four-sided figure from two drag corners, and Shift holds it square while Alt/Option draws it from its centre outward. Radius rounds the corners before you draw, and the shape it produces is a Live Shape whose four corner radii can afterwards be set independently — Alt/Option-drag the on-canvas radius control to break one corner out of the link. The separate Rounded Rectangle tool was removed in Photoshop 22.3 because the Radius field on this tool subsumes it. Clicking the canvas with no drag opens a Create Rectangle dialog so an exact width, height and corner radius can be typed instead of dragged.

Shape is the default.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Figures/Shape.tsx:272` |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the drag to a square drag box, which is a square for the Rectangle tool and a circle for the Ellipse tool.
- **Alt** — Draws from the centre outward, so the press point is the middle of the shape rather than one corner.
- **Space** — Repositions the shape while the drag is still in progress, without changing its size.

**Shortcuts**

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. The six geometric figures share one app tool name and differ only by their figure, so U keeps whichever of them is active rather than forcing the rectangle; the Custom Shape tool carries its own tool name, and U from there lands on the rectangle. Nothing happens until an image is open.

**In this app:** `partial` — The drag geometry, Shift, Alt and the corner radius all behave as they do in Photoshop, and the radius is clamped to half the shorter side exactly as a rounded rectangle must be. That is the whole of what is right, and the divergences below are why the verdict is `partial` and not `implemented`. The three the group carries apply to the Rectangle verbatim: Path mode does not create a path, Pixels mode rasterizes onto a new layer exactly as Shape mode does rather than painting into the active one, and the options bar shares one colour with the rest of the app rather than carrying its own Fill and Stroke swatches, so the fill is whatever the global background colour currently is and there is no way to turn the stroke off at all. The Rectangle adds two divergences of its own, and the first is a default rather than a gap: it seeds a 5 px stroke where Photoshop seeds 1 px, so an untouched rectangle is drawn five times as heavy as Photoshop would draw it. The Radius slider runs 0–250 px with no numeric entry on the bar, and only the rectangle gets a radius — the app gates the whole control on this figure. Fill and Stroke are on the bar, then, and `partial` in the table above is the honest reading of them: what the app renders is a single wired `Filled` checkbox over its one shared colour, and it is the separate swatches with their None / Solid / Gradient / Pattern menu that are missing, not the controls. The mode group, the stroke width, the stroke type and the opacity each diverge from Photoshop’s control in the same way, and the path weight, the pixel-mode blend mode, the anti-alias control, the three path-operation rows and the gear are absent outright. A bare click is where this figure is at its closest: Adobe’s one documented sentence is this figure’s own, and all four of the fields it names — Width, Height, corner radii and align from centre — are in the app’s Create Rectangle dialog, so nothing is left over on this figure. The corner radius is seeded from the bar’s live slider and applied to the layer being created, so a radius typed in the dialog does not rewrite the slider behind the user’s back. What diverges is the entry point rather than the fields: `Shape W&H` is a control on Photoshop’s bar and this app’s bar has none, so here the exact geometry is reachable only by opening the dialog with a click.

### Ellipse Tool

`ellipse`

Drag-defined ellipse or circle drawn as a shape layer, a work path, or a filled pixel region.

The Ellipse tool inscribes an ellipse in the drag box; Shift holds it a circle, and Alt/Option draws it from its centre outward. It has no Corner Radius, because an ellipse has no corners, and the field does not appear in the bar. No desktop Adobe page enumerating the Ellipse tool’s bar was found, so that this matches Photoshop is a judgment rather than a documented match. The result is a Live Shape whose width, height and angle stay editable in the Properties panel. Clicking without dragging opens a Create Ellipse dialog for exact dimensions.

### Line Tool

`line`

Drag-defined straight line or arrow, drawn as a shape layer, a work path, or a filled pixel region.

The Line tool drags a single straight segment between two points, and Shift snaps the segment to the nearest multiple of 45 degrees so it lands on a compass bearing. Its colour is the Stroke, not the Fill, because a line is an open path with a stroke and no interior to fill. The Arrowheads panel adds Start and End toggles, with Width, Length and Concavity to size them; Adobe documents it as a section of the Contextual Task Bar (Window > Contextual Task Bar), not a field in the options bar. The end caps are Butt, Round or Square.

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the line angle to a multiple of 45 degrees, so the segment lands on a compass bearing.
- **Alt** — Draws from the centre outward, so the press point is the middle of the shape rather than one corner.
- **Space** — Repositions the shape while the drag is still in progress, without changing its size.

**Shortcuts**

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. The six geometric figures share one app tool name and differ only by their figure, so U keeps whichever of them is active rather than forcing the rectangle; the Custom Shape tool carries its own tool name, and U from there lands on the rectangle. Nothing happens until an image is open.

**In this app:** `partial` — The drag is the tool, and the drag is right: `normalizeShapeGeometry` routes the line figure to `snapLineGeometry`, which quantizes the drag angle to `LINE_ANGLE_STEP` — `Math.PI / 4` — so a Shift-drag snaps to a multiple of 45 degrees exactly as Adobe specifies, and unlike every other figure the line is not squared by Shift. The two things that are missing are the arrowheads and the shape of the bar. Arrowheads are absent outright — `drawShape` strokes a bare moveTo/lineTo pair, with no start or end cap geometry — which is why a line here can never become an arrow, and that is what keeps the verdict at `partial` rather than `implemented`: the tool that draws arrows does not draw them. The Cap select the app renders for this figure offers Photoshop’s three cap styles but only the Line figure gets one, where Photoshop offers caps for any stroked path, through the Stroke Options panel rather than a bar-level select. A bare click gets no dialog at all on this figure, and that is the contract rather than a gap: Adobe documents the Line tool as a drag and a release and never names a Create Line dialog, so the click refuses on the console instead of opening a dialog Adobe has not got. A line has no Width and Height on Adobe’s side either, so the drag is the only place either can give it a length.

### Triangle Tool

`triangle`

Drag-defined triangle with its apex at the top-centre of the drag box; hold Shift while dragging to constrain it to an equilateral triangle.

The Triangle tool, added in Photoshop 2021 (v22), draws a three-sided figure whose apex sits at the top-centre of the drag box and whose base spans its bottom. Adobe states the drag and the Shift constraint but never the resulting geometry, so reading that box as an isosceles triangle rather than a regular one is this description’s inference, not Adobe’s wording. Shift while dragging is the equilateral constraint — it forces the height to √3⁄2 of the width — and it is not a square-drag aspect snap. Alt/Option draws from the centre, and a single Radius control rounds all three corners together, because this tool has no per-corner radius handles. The tool is a shortcut for the Polygon tool at three sides, not a separate shape vocabulary.

- **Alt** — Draws from the centre outward, so the press point is the middle of the shape rather than one corner.
- **Space** — Repositions the shape while the drag is still in progress, without changing its size.

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. Nothing happens until an image is open.

**In this app:** `partial` — The geometry is wrong in the specific way the premise correction warns about. The app inscribes a regular three-sided polygon in the drag box, so a wide drag yields a squat isosceles-looking triangle only by accident, and Shift squares the drag box instead of forcing equilateral — for a 3-gon inscribed in a square box, that is not h = √3⁄2 · w. Because the figure is built by the shared triangle/polygon branch, its Radius field is both absent from the bar and unimplemented in the renderer, so its corners can never be rounded. The Shift behaviour is version-dependent in wording only: the equilateral constraint has been the tool’s Shift since 2021 (v22), and later versions add the persistent Equilateral checkbox to the gear menu. A bare click opens the app’s Create Triangle dialog with Width, Height and From Center, so of the five things Adobe documents for this figure’s click dialog — Width, Height, Corner Radius, Equilateral and From Center — three can be typed here and two are gaps. Equilateral is absent outright, and it is the same gap the Shift row above reaches from the other direction. Corner Radius is withheld rather than absent: `drawShape` reads `cornerRadius` in its rectangle branch only, so a triangle field would take a value and round nothing, and this figure’s corners cannot be rounded here either way.

### Polygon Tool

`polygon`

Drag-defined polygon of any number of sides, with the side count set before the draw; the star of a given point count is a separate tool.

The Polygon tool is drag-defined, not a click-to-place-vertices tool: Adobe says to click and drag on the canvas, and the ordinary reading of that is a regular n-gon inscribed in the drag box — the regularity is this description’s inference, not Adobe’s wording. Sides sets the n before the draw and defaults to 5. The star is not this tool’s to draw in the current release: Adobe’s tools list puts a separate Star tool in the same shapes group, and the star attributes — the number of points, the Inner Radius that sets the depth of the indents and the Outer Radius that sets the length of the spikes — are documented on that tool, in the Contextual Task Bar and the Properties panel. Shift constrains proportions, Alt/Option draws from the centre — though a polygon is already centred in its drag box — and third-party reports say Control/Cmd-drag rotates it; the Adobe pages reviewed here do not confirm that gesture. A single Radius control rounds every corner at once. The result is a Live Shape whose side count stays editable in the Properties panel.

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the drag to a box whose sides match, so the polygon comes out symmetrical; reported to be off by default in the gear menu, which is a third-party account rather than an Adobe sentence. THIS APP DIVERGES: Shift squares the drag box rather than constraining the polygon's own proportions.
- **Alt** — Draws from the centre outward, so the press point is the middle of the shape rather than one corner.
- **Space** — Repositions the shape while the drag is still in progress, without changing its size.

**Shortcuts**

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. The six geometric figures share one app tool name and differ only by their figure, so U keeps whichever of them is active rather than forcing the rectangle; the Custom Shape tool carries its own tool name, and U from there lands on the rectangle. Nothing happens until an image is open.

**In this app:** `partial` — The load-bearing premise is right here: the app builds a regular n-gon in the drag box, so the drag-defined model is already correct, and the side count is a real setting seeded at 5, matching Photoshop — though the regularity itself is an inference from Adobe's drag instruction rather than something Adobe states. Sides is on the bar for this figure, takes the integers 3 through 100 — Adobe's own floor and ceiling — and persists per figure. The separate Star figure now owns its points and Star Ratio controls, so Polygon does not claim those controls. The `[` and `]` rows Photoshop gives this tool are still absent from the table above, but the reason has changed and the old one would now be a falsehood: the side count does exist at runtime, and the gap is that the app's bracket keys reach only the eight tools that carry a tip Size, so they have nothing to act on. The Radius field is withheld from the bar for this figure, matching the app's rectangle-only gate but not Photoshop, which third-party sources say offers it. Shift squares the drag box rather than constraining the polygon's own proportions, and the Control-drag rotation the Polygon tool has over every other figure is not implemented — which is why `Control` is absent from the `modifiers` table above: in this app holding it while drawing a polygon changes nothing. A bare click opens the app's Create Polygon dialog with Width, Height and From Center, and no field of this figure's own geometry is in it: the dialog commits the bar's current Sides rather than taking one of its own. The polygon is the one figure whose full click-dialog list Adobe published and then stopped publishing: a January 2021 archive of `drawing-shapes.html` names Symmetric, Number of Sides, Corner Radius, Star Ratio and Smooth Star Indents beside Width & Height and From Center, and the current page carries none of them — and of those the renderer reads only Number of Sides, from the bar rather than from the dialog, because no star or indent argument is read at all. Those are gaps rather than withheld fields, and the dialog is not where any of them can be closed.

### Star Tool

`star`

Drag-defined star with a configurable number of points and alternating outer and inner radii.

The Star tool draws a customizable star from the Shapes tool group. Adobe documents Number of Points, Outer Radius, Inner Radius and Corner Radius, plus Fill and Stroke. Third-party reports say Shift constrains proportions, but the Adobe pages reviewed here do not specify this gesture. Alt/Option draws from the centre. The app exposes points through the existing 3–100 Polygon bounds and represents the two radii as a Star Ratio / Indent percentage.

**In this app:** `partial` — The Star is implemented as another figure in the shared shape processor. Its path alternates outer and inner vertices, points default to 5, and the Star Ratio / Indent control reaches the renderer. Shape, Path and Pixels modes, Fill/Stroke behaviour, Shift constraint and Alt-from-center are inherited from the existing family. ### Custom Shape Tool

`custom-shape`

Draws a preset vector graphic from Photoshop's shape library, or one you define from a path.

The Custom Shape tool draws any of the vector presets in Photoshop’s shape library — a library that includes the Leaf Trees, Wild Animals, Boats and Flowers groups, with the full set reached through Legacy Shapes and More in the Shapes panel. Those four were the default loaded groups in a 2020 account, and Adobe Community threads from 2019–2021 report that the picker changed and moved them behind Legacy Shapes and More, so what a current install shows on first launch is not established here. Third-party accounts, not Adobe’s own documentation, say this is the only shape tool whose Shift constraint preserves the drawn shape’s own aspect ratio rather than squaring the drag box, so a recognisable graphic comes out undistorted. Its Path Operations menu is where the boolean work happens: New Shape Layer, Combine Shapes, Subtract Front Shape — which Adobe’s 2022 wording calls Subtract From Shape Area — Intersect Shape Areas, Exclude Overlapping Shapes, and Merge Shape Components, which converts the live shape into a plain path and warns you that it can no longer be edited component by component. No single Adobe page enumerates that whole set. Any path — drawn with the Pen tool, made from a shape layer, or produced by converting text to a path — becomes a new preset through Edit ▸ Define Custom Shape, and Preset Manager saves and loads the result as a `.csh` file.

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Draws the preset at its own original width-to-height ratio instead of filling the drag box — a third-party account, echoed by an Adobe training partner’s modifier cheat sheet and stated in no Adobe help page.
- **Alt** — Draws from the centre outward, so the press point is the middle of the shape rather than one corner.
