**Shortcuts**

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. The six geometric figures share one app tool name and differ only by their figure, so U keeps whichever of them is active rather than forcing the rectangle; the Custom Shape tool carries its own tool name, and U from there lands on the rectangle. Nothing happens until an image is open.

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Registered, selectable, and a dead button. The processor row declares commit: 'unimplemented' and wires the shared unimplemented rasterizer, the tools map renders PlaceholderTool with a TODO badge, and the only state the settings hold is the tool name — no shape preset, no fill, no geometry. The placeholder panel does list Photoshop’s real control names for this bar, so the six chips a user sees are the genuine Photoshop set rather than placeholders for placeholders: Tool Mode, Fill, Stroke, W/H, Shape Picker, Path Operations. That is why those six rows read `inert` and not `missing` — the names are on screen and nothing is wired behind any of them, which is the exact shape the `inert` status exists for. The three rows that were `partial` above are also `missing` rather than partial, but for the opposite reason: Stroke width, Stroke type and Opacity have no chip in this tool's list at all, and the real shape bar that carries them never renders here, because this tool is absent from the canvas dispatch that gives the other five figures their gesture surface. It is a `display: none` area, so the three modifiers named above — Shift, Alt and Space — are bound to nothing either, and the app’s Shift constraint, which squares the drag box for every figure except the line, has no drag to apply to. That is also the whole of the app side of the Shape W&H row: a bare click opens a Create <Figure> dialog on the five figures that mount `ShapeToolArea`, and this tool mounts `DummyToolArea` instead, so none of that runs here and a click with no drag does nothing rather than opening a sized dialog. Subtract needs a multi-subpath model with a fill rule, which a single convex outline cannot express, so the boolean operations are not a bar toggle away; they are a data-model decision first.

### Shape Tool (the Tools panel group; no entry by that name)

`shape`

Draws a vector shape, a path, or a filled pixel region, and stamps it onto its own shape layer.

Adobe’s Tools panel has no entry named “Shape Tool”, so there is no Photoshop tool behind this one: the panel groups seven separate tools — Rectangle, Ellipse, Triangle, Polygon, Star, Line and Custom Shape — behind a single group icon, and the Star arrived as a tool of its own in 26.10. Whichever of the seven is active, the three-button Mode group at the left of the options bar decides what a drag commits — a filled shape layer with a vector mask, a work path with no pixels at all, or a rasterized region painted straight into the active layer. Fill and Stroke are set independently of each other and of the drawing mode, so the same rectangle can be a solid block, a hairline outline, or an outline over a gradient. The drawn shape stays a Live Shape, so its fill, stroke, corner radius and dimensions remain editable from the Properties panel long after the drag.

**Options bar**

| Control                               | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | In this app                                                      |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mode                                  | The first of the two controls Adobe names Mode, and the one at the left of the bar: the three-button drawing-mode group, where Shape creates a filled shape layer, Path creates a vector path with no pixels, and Pixels rasterizes the shape straight into the current layer. Shape is the default.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Figures/Shape.tsx:272` |
| Fill                                  | The interior colour of the shape, as a swatch offering None, Solid Color, Gradient or Pattern. Fill and Stroke are independent: a shape can have a fill and no stroke, or the reverse. THIS APP DIVERGES: No separate Fill swatch with None/Solid/Gradient/Pattern menu. Only a single wired "Filled" checkbox over one shared app colour — the fill is whatever the global background colour currently is, and there is no way to choose None, Gradient, or Pattern fill independently.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Figures/Shape.tsx:409` |
| Stroke                                | The colour of the outline, as a second swatch with the same None / Solid Color / Gradient / Pattern choices. Set it to None to draw a fill with no outline. THIS APP DIVERGES: no separate Stroke swatch or stroke-off control. Its single "Filled" checkbox controls fill only; stroke is always drawn using the app stroke color and width. The app seeds a 5 px stroke where Photoshop seeds 1 px, so an untouched shape is drawn five times as heavy as Photoshop would draw it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Figures/Shape.tsx:290` |

**Shortcuts**

- `U` — Selects the shapes tool group. The six geometric figures share one app tool name and differ only by their figure, so U keeps whichever of them is active rather than forcing the rectangle; the Custom Shape tool carries its own tool name, and U from there lands on the rectangle. Nothing happens until an image is open.
- `Shift+U` — Cycles to the next tool in the shapes tool group. The rail flyout and keyboard cycle hold seven entries — rectangle, ellipse, line, triangle, polygon, star and Custom Shape. The group closes, so the press after Custom Shape returns to the Rectangle.

**In this app:** `partial` — The Star entry is now present in the app’s seven-entry shapes fly-out (`toolbar-mapping.ts`), and the `shape` registry entry this description hangs off remains the group container rather than a tool the rail displays by itself. The processor is live and every drag commits a layer, so nothing here is a placeholder, but the group diverges from Photoshop in three further ways worth naming. Path mode does not create a path: the mode only suppresses the fill inside the rasterizer, so a Path-mode shape still rasterizes to a layer with a stroke. Pixels mode is not a mode of its own: the figure is rasterized and put on a new layer exactly as in Shape mode, where Photoshop paints straight into the active layer and leaves nothing new in the Layers panel. And the options bar shares one colour with the rest of the app rather than carrying its own Fill and Stroke swatches, so the fill is whatever the global background colour currently is and there is no way to turn the stroke off at all. A click with no drag is the group’s one place where the app meets Adobe head-on: Adobe documents the click dialog in a single sentence, for the rectangle — "Click on the canvas to bring up the Create Rectangle dialog" — and the app opens a `CreateShapeDialog` modal for every figure except the Line, titled per figure, offering Width, Height and From Center, plus a Corner Radius field on the rectangle that is seeded from that figure’s live Radius slider and applied to the layer being created rather than to the bar. The click itself commits nothing: OK is the only commit, Cancel, the backdrop, the header × and Escape all close without one, and OK is disabled outright while a dimension is under 1 px. The Line is the exception and is excluded by contract rather than by taste — Adobe documents the drag and the release for it and never names a Create Line dialog, so a click there refuses on the console instead of inventing a dialog Adobe has not got. What the dialog still leaves out is per-figure rather than shared, and the triangle and polygon entries below each name their own figure’s gaps against what this renderer can honour.

## Pen and path

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/pen.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/pen.notes.md).

### Pen Tool

`pen` · **P**

Draws precise vector paths from click-placed anchor points, with draggable direction handles for the curves between them.

The Pen tool builds a path of straight and curved segments by clicking to place anchor points and dragging to pull out the direction handles that shape each curve. It draws no pixels: Path mode creates a work path in the Paths panel, which draws nothing on the canvas and can be stroked, filled or loaded as a selection later. The drawing mode group decides which of those you get — Shape makes a filled, stroked shape layer, Path makes the work path, Pixels rasterizes straight onto the current layer. Every path-construction decision the tool makes is a decision about vector geometry, which is why it stays sharp at any zoom and survives scaling that would blur a painted line.

**Options bar**

| Control                   | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | In this app                                                             |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mode                      | The three-button drawing-mode group at the left of the bar, and the control that decides what the rest of the bar shows. The current Pen settings page tabulates the values as Shape, Path and Pixels, and Adobe’s older drawing page names the same three buttons Shape Layers, Paths and Fill Pixels. Shape creates a shape layer with a vector mask; Path creates a work path that can be stroked or filled later; Pixels creates a rasterized shape directly on the current layer. The Fill, Stroke and Stroke width controls exist in Shape mode; the Operation, Path arrangement and Path alignment controls exist in Path mode. The app names this chip "Tool Mode". | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Fill                      | Fill color: a swatch that sets the color, pattern or gradient used to fill the shape, and can be set to None. Shape mode only. Double-clicking the swatch opens the color menu.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Stroke                    | Stroke color: a swatch setting the color of the shape outline, with a width and a stroke type (solid, dashed or dotted, with Inside/Center/Outside alignment, Butt/Round/Square caps and a corner treatment). Shape mode only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Operation                 | Path mode only. The path area option that decides how the component you are about to draw combines with the components already in the path: Add To Path Area, Subtract From Path Area, Intersect Path Areas, or Exclude Overlapping Path Areas. A shape tool may hold Shift to temporarily pick Add and Alt (Windows) or Option (macOS) to temporarily pick Subtract. The app labels this "Path Operations", and that is the single chip of that name in the list it renders — so this row, and not the Path Selection tool’s control below, is what the chip stands for.                                                                                                   | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Path Operations           | The Path Selection tool’s drop-down of the same four overlap modes, named Combine Shapes, Subtract From Shape Area, Intersect Shape Areas and Exclude Overlapping Shape Areas, plus Merge Shape Components, which fuses every overlapping component into one. It acts on an existing path component rather than on the one being drawn, so the Pen family shares the vocabulary without owning the control. The app’s bar does not carry it: the one "Path Operations" chip on it stands for the Pen’s own Operation control above, and nothing on the bar names this one — which is a divergence from Photoshop, not a rendering fact.                                     | `missing`                                                               |
| Path alignment            | Align and distribute path components, the same way the alignment controls work for layers: align selected components, or distribute at least three. The app labels this "Alignment".                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Path arrangement          | The stacking order used when several paths are present, so that a later path draws over an earlier one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `missing`                                                               |
| Path thickness (Weight)   | Sets the width in pixels of the on-canvas line that represents the path. A display aid only: it has no effect on a stroke applied later, and on the pen family it lives in the Set additional pen and path options flyout, where newer releases label it Weight.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `missing`                                                               |
| Path color                | The other half of the same Path Options panel, and Adobe states the pair as one control: "Path options: Thickness and Color". The color of the on-canvas line that represents the path, set in the same Set additional pen and path options flyout as the thickness. A display aid only, for the same reason — it changes nothing about the path and has no effect on a stroke applied later.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `missing`                                                               |
| Selection… / Mask / Shape | The group at the right end of the bar that converts the path you have already drawn: Selection… loads it as a selection through the Make Selection dialog (which is where feathering and anti-aliasing are set), Mask turns it into a vector mask, and Shape fills it into a new shape layer. These act on the current path, not on the next one you draw. The app names this chip "Make Selection".                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Auto Add/Delete           | A checkbox, on by default, that makes the Pen tool morph as you move over an existing path: over a segment it becomes the Add Anchor Point tool, over an anchor point it becomes the Delete Anchor Point tool. It also stops selecting an anchor point from changing the shape of the path. Deselect it to start a new path on top of an existing one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Rubber Band               | Live preview of the segment you are about to commit, drawn between the pointer and the pending anchor point as you move, so you can see the path before you click. Lives in the Set additional pen and path options flyout at the right of the bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                                               |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the segment being placed to 45-degree angles.
- **Alt** — Converts a smooth point to a corner point when you click it, and unhinges a direction handle from its opposite so you can set the two independently while dragging a curve.
- **Ctrl/Command** — Temporarily activates the Direct Selection tool while you draw, so that you can adjust segments you have already drawn.

**Shortcuts**

- `P` — Selects the Pen tool, or keeps whichever Pen-family tool is already active — with the Freeform Pen or the Curvature Pen selected, P selects that one rather than jumping back to the Pen. Nothing happens until an image is open.
- `Shift+P` — Cycles through the tools nested in the Pen group.
- `Ctrl+Enter` — Loads the current path as a selection, the same as the Load path as a selection button at the bottom of the Paths panel.
- `Ctrl+Alt` — Activates the Convert Point tool temporarily while the Direct Selection tool is selected, when the pointer is over an anchor point.

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. The processor exists but is the shared stub that returns a null bitmap, and its commit kind is unimplemented, so a drag over the canvas produces no layer, no history state and no durable operation. The app registers this tool, but it has no options bar of its own: the panel it renders is the shared amber placeholder with a TODO badge, and no control below is a working control — the ones that panel names are its chips, and the rest are absent from it entirely. The tool carries a single state key, its own name, so there is no setting behind any chip to be out of range. Selecting the tool changes nothing on the canvas — there is no path layer, no anchor point and no stroke to place. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. The app does bind the letter P and Shift+P cycling for the Pen group — and those two keys are the whole of the Pen's Photoshop chrome here, along with a tool-preset entry for the tool. Neither of the two shortcuts the bar above names that act on a path, `Ctrl+Enter` and `Ctrl+Alt`, is bound anywhere in the app. The options table above is the Shape and Path mode bar; Adobe's own enumeration of the Pixels-mode controls — `Mode`, `Opacity` and `Anti-alias` — carries the scope line "When using the Line tool or other shape tools", and the Pen settings page confirms that the Pen has a Pixels mode without ever listing what that mode's bar contains, so no row above describes Pixels mode and none is invented for it.

### Freeform Pen Tool

`freeform-pen`

Draws a path freehand, placing anchor points and fitting bezier handles to the stroke as you drag instead of clicking them one at a time.

The Freeform Pen takes a single drag and turns it into a path, so it is the tool for tracing something by hand rather than plotting it. The raw trail is simplified on release into as few anchor points as fit it, mixing straight corner points with curved ones. Turn on Magnetic and the trail stops following your hand and starts following the image: the live segment snaps to the strongest edge within Width, and fastening points are dropped along the border to anchor what you have already traced. It is the one Pen-family tool you can pick up in a photograph and use immediately, and the one to reach for when the precision of the standard Pen is more than the job needs.

**Options bar**

| Control                   | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | In this app                                                             |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |

The app names this chip "Tool Mode".                                                                                                                                                                     | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Fill                      | Fill color for the shape. Shape mode only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Stroke                    | Stroke color, width and type for the shape outline. Shape mode only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Curve Fit                 | A single numeric field, 0.5 to 10 pixels, that sets the tolerance the fitted path is simplified to: a low value follows your hand closely and yields a dense, spiky path with many anchor points, a high value yields a coarse one with few. It is one number, not a menu of fit styles. Enter it from the inverted-arrow flyout beside the shape buttons. | `missing`                                                               |
| Magnetic                  | The checkbox that turns edge snapping on. With it off the tool is a plain freehand pen; with it on, the last active segment snaps to the strongest edge in the image, using the same Width / Contrast / Frequency / Stylus Pressure controls the Magnetic Lasso documents. The cursor carries a magnet while it is active.                                 | `missing`                                                               |
| Align Edges               | The neighboring control in the same flyout, which straightens a traced segment against the edge it snapped to. It is unavailable while the Freeform Pen is the active tool.                                                                                                                                                                                | `missing`                                                               |
| Selection… / Mask / Shape | The group at the right end of the bar that converts the path you have already drawn into a selection, a vector mask or a shape layer. The app names this chip "Make Selection".                                                                                                                                                                            | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Path color                | The color half of the Path Options panel — Adobe states the pair as one control, "Path options: Thickness and Color" — which sets the color of the on-canvas line that represents the path. A display aid only, in the same Set additional pen and path options flyout as the thickness, and it has no effect on a stroke applied later.                   | `missing`                                                               |
| Rubber Band               | Live preview of the pending path segment. Lives in the Set additional pen and path options flyout.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                                               |

**Shortcuts**

- `P` — Selects the Pen tool, or keeps the Freeform Pen if it is the Pen-family tool already active. P never selects the Freeform Pen from another tool — from anywhere outside the three pens it is the Pen tool that comes up.
- `Shift+P` — Cycles through the tools nested in the Pen group.

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented, and the placeholder config is itself wrong for this tool in a way a test pins. The chip list the Freeform Pen actually renders is the standard Pen's — the config entry written for the Freeform Pen, with its Magnetic and Curve Fit chips, is dead configuration that no tool reaches, and a test asserts that it stays dead. So the two controls that are this tool's entire reason for existing are the two it does not even name in its bar. The app registers this tool, but it has no options bar of its own: the panel it renders is the shared amber placeholder with a TODO badge, and no control below is a working control — the ones that panel names are its chips, and the rest are absent from it entirely. The tool carries a single state key, its own name, so there is no setting behind any chip to be out of range. Selecting the tool changes nothing on the canvas — there is no path layer, no anchor point and no stroke to place. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box.

### Curvature Pen Tool

`curvature-pen`

Draws smooth curved paths from plain clicks, computing the curve for you so there are no direction handles to manage at all.

The Curvature Pen is Illustrator’s Curvature tool ported into Photoshop, and it exists to remove the part of the standard Pen people find hardest. You click to place points; Photoshop fits the curve through them and keeps fitting as you add more, so a path is a sequence of smooth points and you never see, drag or think about a bezier handle. You shape it by pushing and pulling whole segments, and you switch one point between straight and curved with a double-click. Because the fit is continuous it will not give you the deliberately angular corner the standard Pen can, nor the deliberately flat run of a long handle; it is for the organic outline, and the standard Pen for everything else. It arrived in Photoshop CC 2018 (19.0) and is the newest tool in this family.

| Control                   | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | In this app                                                             |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mode                      | The same three-button drawing-mode group as the standard Pen — Shape, Path, Pixels — and the control that decides what the rest of the bar shows. The app names this chip "Tool Mode".                                                                                      | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Fill                      | Fill color for the shape, and it is set to None for the tracing workflow the tool is usually used in. Shape mode only.                                                                                                                                                      | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Stroke                    | Stroke color, width and type for the shape outline, also set to None for pure path tracing. | Path color                | The other half of the Path Options panel Adobe states as one control — "Path options: Thickness and Color" — the color of the on-canvas line representing the path, set in that same flyout beside the thickness. A display aid only, for the same reason the thickness is. | `missing`                                                               |
| Align Edges               | The neighboring control in that flyout, which straightens a segment against the edge it snapped to. It is reported as unavailable while the Curvature Pen is the active tool.                                                                                               | `missing`                                                               |

The app names this chip "Make Selection".                                                                                             | `inert` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/toolbarPlaceholderConfig.ts:23` |
| Rubber Band               | Live preview of the pending path, so the curve Photoshop is about to fit is visible before you click.                                                                                                                                                                       | `missing`                                                               |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Constrains the path you are placing to 90° and 45° angles.
- **Alt/Option** — Creates a corner point where you click — the same result as double-clicking a point, which switches it between straight and curved.

**Shortcuts**

- `P` — Selects the Pen tool, or keeps the Curvature Pen if it is the Pen-family tool already active. P never selects the Curvature Pen from another tool — from anywhere outside the three pens it is the Pen tool that comes up.
- `Shift+P` — Cycles through the tools nested in the Pen group.
- `Esc` — Stops drawing the current path.

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented, and the placeholder config is wrong for this tool the same way it is wrong for the Freeform Pen: the chip list this tool renders is the standard Pen's, and the config entry written for the Curvature Pen is dead configuration that no tool reaches. That entry also lists Magnetic and Curve Fit, which are the Freeform Pen's controls and not this tool's. The app registers this tool, but it has no options bar of its own: the panel it renders is the shared amber placeholder with a TODO badge, and no control below is a working control — the ones that panel names are its chips, and the rest are absent from it entirely. The tool carries a single state key, its own name, so there is no setting behind any chip to be out of range. Selecting the tool changes nothing on the canvas — there is no path layer, no anchor point and no stroke to place. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. `Esc` is named above as Photoshop’s way of stopping a path, and the app binds no `Escape` for this tool or any other in the family: its five `Escape` handlers belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box.

### Add Anchor Point Tool

`add-anchor-point`

Inserts an anchor point into an existing path exactly where you click on a segment.

The Add Anchor Point tool subdivides a path. It only means anything against a path that already exists and is selected in the Paths panel, which is why it is a Tools-panel entry rather than a mode of the Pen: the standard Pen reaches the same result on its own when Auto Add/Delete is on, and this tool is the explicit version for when you want to add a point without switching tools mid-drag. Clicking a segment inserts a point there; dragging while you click reshapes the path as you add, so you can bend the line and place the new point in one gesture. The point it adds is a smooth point with direction handles, which is why the segments either side of it can change shape rather than merely being cut in two.

_Photoshop gives this tool no options bar of its own._

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. Photoshop documents no options-bar control specific to this tool — selecting it shows the Pen group's bar, so every control on it belongs to the Pen and none is the Add Anchor Point tool's own — which is why its options table is empty. What the app does render is the standard Pen's chip list, on a panel with a TODO badge, over a tool whose registered processor is the same shared stub that returns a null bitmap the whole Pen family uses, over state that is nothing but its own name, and over no Paths panel to select a path in. The app's SidebarLeft gives this tool the same pen-nib icon as the Pen itself, so the three anchor-point tools are visually indistinguishable from it. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. The keyboard is the other half of the gap. The app binds exactly two keys for this family: `P`, which selects the Pen tool or keeps whichever of the three pens is already active, and `Shift+P`, which cycles that same three. The rail’s Pen flyout lists six tools, so the cycle covers three of the six and the three path-modification tools — Add Anchor Point, Delete Anchor Point and Convert Point — are unreachable from any key in the app.

### Delete Anchor Point Tool

`delete-anchor-point`

Removes the anchor point you click from an existing path, and the two segments around it re-solve.

The Delete Anchor Point tool takes a point out of a path that already exists and is selected in the Paths panel. The consequence is the interesting part: the two segments that met at the removed point do not simply join end to end, they are re-fitted across the new span, so deleting a point from a curve usually changes the curve and can smooth out the kink that point was holding. It is the counterpart to the Add Anchor Point tool and, like it, mostly exists so the Pen family is not a three-tool round trip for every edit; the standard Pen reaches it on its own when Auto Add/Delete is on. Note the trap Adobe calls out: the keyboard Delete key is not this tool. It removes the point and the segments joined to it, splitting the path in two.

_Photoshop gives this tool no options bar of its own._

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. Photoshop documents no options-bar control specific to this tool — selecting it shows the Pen group's bar, so every control on it belongs to the Pen and none is the Delete Anchor Point tool's own — which is why its options table is empty. What the app does render is the standard Pen's chip list, on a panel with a TODO badge, over a tool whose registered processor is the same shared stub that returns a null bitmap the whole Pen family uses, over state that is nothing but its own name, and over no Paths panel to select a path in. The app's SidebarLeft gives this tool the same pen-nib icon as the Pen itself. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. The keyboard is the other half of the gap. The app binds exactly two keys for this family: `P`, which selects the Pen tool or keeps whichever of the three pens is already active, and `Shift+P`, which cycles that same three. ### Convert Point Tool

`convert-point`

Converts an anchor point between corner and smooth, with or without independent direction lines.

The Convert Point tool changes the type of a point on a path that already exists and is selected in the Paths panel, and a single drag does three different things depending on what you grabbed. Drag away from a corner point and direction lines appear, making it a smooth point whose handles you then shape. Click a smooth point and it becomes a corner point with no direction lines, so the segments either side leave it independently. Drag one of a smooth point’s direction points and the point stays smooth but the two handles are unhinged, so they can point in different directions — which is what produces an S-curve. The Pen reaches all three with Alt held, and with the Direct Selection tool selected, Ctrl+Alt (Windows) or Command+Option (macOS) over an anchor point reaches this tool without leaving that tool.

_Photoshop gives this tool no options bar of its own._

**Shortcuts**

- `Ctrl+Alt` — Activates the Convert Point tool temporarily while the Direct Selection tool is selected and the pointer is over an anchor point.

**In this app:** `placeholder` — Not implemented. Photoshop documents no options-bar control specific to this tool — selecting it shows the Pen group's bar, so every control on it belongs to the Pen and none is the Convert Point tool's own — which is why its options table is empty. What the app does render is the standard Pen's chip list, on a panel with a TODO badge, over a tool whose registered processor is that same shared null-bitmap stub and over state that is nothing but its own name. This is also one of the tools the durable document refuses: converting a history item that names it is rejected as an unsupported feature rather than silently replayed. It has no gesture surface either. The canvas dispatch turns a tool name into an interaction mode and names none of the six Pen tools in any of its branches, so all six mount the dummy tool area — a `display: none` div — instead of a canvas handler. There is no drag for a modifier to change and no path for a key to act on, which is why none of the modifiers or shortcuts above is bound: the app registers no `Escape` for this family, and the only five `Escape` handlers bound to a tool anywhere in it belong to the lasso (twice), the crop tool, the font picker and the transform box. `Ctrl+Alt` is named above as the way to reach this tool from the Direct Selection tool, and the app registers no Alt-bearing keybinding at all: the five tools that read `altKey` are the shape tool, the elliptical marquee, the eyedropper, the clone stamp and the magnetic lasso, none of which is in this family. The keyboard is the other half of the gap. The app binds exactly two keys for this family: `P`, which selects the Pen tool or keeps whichever of the three pens is already active, and `Shift+P`, which cycles that same three. The rail’s Pen flyout lists six tools, so the cycle covers three of the six and the three path-modification tools — Add Anchor Point, Delete Anchor Point and Convert Point — are unreachable from any key in the app.

## Type and crop

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/type-crop.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/type-crop.notes.md).

### Crop Tool

`crop` · **C**

Frames a document boundary; extending past the image reveals retained pixels. Enter applies; Esc cancels. No Fill, Straighten or Delete Cropped Pixels.

A crop sets a new boundary for the document. Selecting the Crop tool shows a crop box you can drag out and resize by its handles; dragging just outside a corner rotates the image inside the box (Adobe: "Place the pointer a little outside the corner handles and drag to rotate the image. A grid displays inside the crop box and the image rotates behind it"), while dragging inside the box moves the image and leaves the box where it is. Adobe's newer crop page says the opposite on both counts; the behavior asserted here follows the current desktop page and third-party literature. Nothing is committed until you confirm with Enter/Return, the Done button, or a double-click inside the box, and Esc cancels and restores the framing you had before. Photoshop treats the crop as non-destructive until that commit, and it is only irreversible once the commit happens with Delete Cropped Pixels on. This describes Photoshop 2024–2026, where Straight Crop is the tool's default mode and Perspective Crop is a separate tool in the same flyout.

**Options bar**

| Control                      | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | In this app                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Tool Preset picker           | The drop-down at the upper-left of the bar, beside the tool icon, that recalls a saved configuration of the whole bar. Adobe: "You can also select the Tool Presets dropdown menu next to the tool at the upper-left of the Options bar." A crop preset can carry a ratio, or a width, height and resolution.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | `missing`                                                    |
| Aspect ratio menu            | Holding Ratio, W x H x Resolution, Original Ratio, 1 : 1 (Square), 4 : 5 (8 : 10), 5 : 7, 2 : 3 (4 : 6), 16 : 9 and Front Image, plus New Crop Preset… to save the current values and Delete Crop Preset to remove a saved one. Adobe names the first entry Ratio (not "Free") and defines it as cropping freely without a fixed ratio; clicking the Clear button clears the Width, Height and Resolution fields. The app renders a partial list with a Ratio select and Apply/Clear buttons (`Crop.tsx:71`).                                                                                                                                                                             | `partial` — `src/components/ToolbarsRight/Crop/Crop.tsx:71`  |

**Modifiers**

- **Shift** — Two different things, both Adobe's. Dragging a fresh box with it held constrains that box to a square; dragging a corner handle with it held constrains the proportions the box already has. The app implements both via `useRect` (`constrainToSquare: true`).
- **Alt** — Draws the crop box outward from its center, so the opposite edge moves as well. The app implements this via `useRect` (`fromCentre: true`).
- **Alt+Shift** — Constrains the proportions and draws from the center at the same time. The app implements both simultaneously.
- **Ctrl / ⌘** — Two more of Adobe's: held on its own it invokes the Straighten tool without visiting the bar, and held during a drag it temporarily disables snapping to the crop box edge. The app has no Straighten and no snapping to disable.
- **Shift while rotating** — Restricts the rotation to 15-degree increments. The app does not implement rotation snapping.
- **Ctrl while rotating** — Prevents the crop box from shrinking as it rotates. The app does not implement this.

**Shortcuts**

- `C` — Select the Crop tool.
- `Shift+C` — Re-selects the same tool rather than cycling a flyout. Adobe groups four tools on `C` — Perspective Crop, Slice and Slice Select beside the Straight Crop — and this tile holds one entry, so the other three are unreachable.
- `Enter / Return` — Commits the pending crop, the same as the Done/Apply button.
- `Esc` — Cancels the pending crop and restores the previous framing.
- `X` — Switches the crop box orientation between portrait and landscape. Unbound in the app.
- `O` — Cycles the six crop overlay options while the Crop tool is active; the tool-scoped handler takes precedence over the global tonal-tool binding. Implemented.
- `Shift+O` — Flips the orientation of the Triangle and Golden Spiral overlays while the Crop tool is active; other overlays ignore this key. Implemented.
- `Backspace / Delete` — Resets the crop box. Unbound in the app for this tool.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app commits crop as a SET_DOCUMENT_FRAME_ACTION, changing documentFrame rather than trimming layer bitmaps. At angle zero, layer source coordinates are unchanged: after a frame crop, re-entering Crop seeds the current bounds, extending them previews retained off-frame layer pixels, and Apply reveals those pixels without resampling. The workspace compensates its contain-fit zoom when a frame changes, including undo and redo, so existing document pixels keep the same on-screen size; compensation is bounded by the view zoom limits. The live preview clears the current frame to avoid double-compositing translucent layers and budgets at most 4,194,304 backing pixels per frame-sized surface; very large previews may be lower resolution. Rotated crops apply a layer transform. Because overhang geometry is axis-aligned, retained-pixel preview and letterbox guides are suppressed at nonzero rotation; rotated recrops reveal retained content on commit. OVR-1 applies to newly exposed areas with no retained source pixels, regardless of the bottom layer; existing off-frame pixels remain recoverable and are revealed when the document frame expands. Adobe documents Delete Cropped Pixels off, Reveal All/drag recovery, a Background-only limitation, and separate Content-Aware and Generative synthesis features. The app still lacks the Delete Cropped Pixels toggle, Image > Reveal All, Fill, and Generative Expand. Retention across save/reopen or flattened export is unverified.

### Horizontal Type Tool

`text` · **T**

Creates raster text layers; a 3 CSS px drag threshold distinguishes point from paragraph type. Unlike Photoshop, text is not live vector type.

Photoshop's Type tools create live, vector-based type: glyph outlines re-rendered from the font, so a type layer stays resolution-independent and editable until deliberately rasterized. Clicking places point type (independent lines, no wrap); dragging a bounding box places paragraph type (lines wrap and reflow on resize). Type can also flow along an open or closed work path, or fill the inside of a closed shape. Paragraph settings — alignment, justification, indents and hyphenation — apply to paragraph type only. The anti-aliasing pull-down (None, Sharp, Crisp, Strong, Smooth; Sharp by default) was on the type options bar until Photoshop 26.10 (community-reported); it is now reached from the Character panel, the layer's properties, and the Type menu. This app has no live type: each committed text presentation is rasterized via `fillText` into a layer-sized OffscreenCanvas. The durable engine re-runs the creator from retained args so characters survive there; the runtime renderer uses `layer.bitmap` so scaling resamples pixels.

**Shortcuts**

- `T` — Select the Type tool.
- `Shift+T` — Re-selects the same tool rather than cycling a flyout. Adobe groups four tools on `T` — Horizontal Type, Vertical Type, Horizontal Type Mask and Vertical Type Mask — and this tile holds one entry, so two of the four are unreachable and the other two are one keypress away on a different tile that does not exist.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app's type layer is baked pixels, not live type. `renderText` paints the string into a 2D context with `fillText`, and the text creator hands back a single OffscreenCanvas, so what reaches the Layers panel is a bitmap. On the runtime path the layer renderer re-runs a tool's creator only for the six shape tools; text is not among them, so the visible canvas, undo replay and the PSD writer all draw `layer.bitmap` and enlarging a text layer rescales those pixels where a Photoshop type layer re-renders at the new size. The durable path is the exception: the durable materializer re-runs the text creator from the retained args, so the characters survive in one of the two engines and are re-derivable there. There are two kinds of type layer, `kind: 'point' | 'paragraph'`, distinguished by a 3 CSS px drag threshold (`POINT_TYPE_MAX_DRAG_PX`) on the pointer's travel in client pixels (not the box extent). A press that travels ≤3 px on both axes places point type; anything further places paragraph type. Adobe distinguishes the two by intent (click vs drag) and documents no threshold, no minimum box size, and nothing about which way a box grows — all three are this app's own. The threshold is applied by the Text tool, NOT by `useRect`. A press inside an existing draft or on its handles is a move/resize and does not reclassify the kind. A second placement while a draft is open commits the first draft (`commitDirtyTool` via `flushSync`) before placing the new one — Adobe commits on tool switch, panel click, or menu command. Placeholder text (`Lorem ipsum`) is seeded only on a fresh placement, not on a move/resize (which would overwrite user text). Paragraph boxes are forced to at least 1 px wide to avoid a zero-width throw in `createLayerSource`. Clicking an existing committed text layer hydrates its source into the tool args and opens the in-place editor (`beginTextLayerEdit`). Small Caps is previewed in the draft via a canvas overlay (`publishSmallCapsTextDraftPreview`) that renders with the same `renderText` used at commit. The overflow indicator (red `+`) is drawn in the draft when paragraph text overflows its box (`drawOverflowIndicator`). Escape commits by default (no preference to flip). No Font Style, no per-character color, no warp, no path type, no Character/Paragraph panels. The `TextOrientation` button is absent (Vertical Type and Type Mask tools are not implemented).

## Move, transform and adjustments

Long-form research, provenance and unverified claims: [`src/tools/descriptions/transform.notes.md`](../src/tools/descriptions/transform.notes.md).

### Move Tool

`reposition` · **V**

Photoshop's Move tool (V) drags layers, selections and artboards around the document, and hosts the transform box Free Transform hangs off.

The Move tool is how content gets placed. Select it, press on a layer, a selection or an artboard, and drag: the layer follows the pointer and settles when the button comes up, so a single drag is a single undo step. It is also the entry point to everything geometric — with Show Transform Controls checked, the same bounding box appears and dragging its handles scales, skews and rotates the layer, which is exactly the state Cmd+T enters. Auto-Select makes the tool pick the layer under the pointer instead of requiring a trip to the Layers panel, and Alt-dragging a layer moves a duplicate of it rather than the original.

**Options bar**

| Control                    | Photoshop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | In this app                                            |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Tool Preset Picker         | The tool icon at the far left of the options bar with a flyout arrow. Clicking it lists that tool's saved presets; Control-clicking it (Command-clicking on macOS) opens a two-item menu — Reset Tool, which returns the current tool's options to their defaults, and Reset All Tools, which does the same for every tool. It is the escape hatch for the fact that a tool's options are the ones you last used, not the ones it shipped with.                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | `missing`                                              |
| Auto-Select                | Checkbox that, when on, resolves the target by hit test: the tool selects the topmost layer that actually has pixels under the cursor, rather than moving whichever layer happens to be active. THIS APP DIVERGES: No checkbox rendered. The tool ALWAYS resolves the layer under the pointer by hit test and makes it active — Auto-Select: Layer is permanently ON with no way to disable, and no Group/Layer menu exists.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | `partial` — `src/components/Main/MoveToolArea.tsx:178` |
| Auto-Select: Group / Layer | Menu beside the Auto-Select checkbox choosing what the hit test resolves to. Layer takes the individual layer under the pointer; Group takes the whole layer group that layer belongs to, so a click anywhere on a grouped child moves the group. THIS APP DIVERGES: No Group/Layer menu. Clicking a grouped child always selects the individual layer, never the group.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | `missing`                                              |
| Show Transform Controls    | Checkbox that displays transform handles on the selected layer without entering Free Transform; dragging a handle starts the transform. THIS APP DIVERGES: No checkbox or Photoshop numeric transform fields/reference point. The app uses a resize rectangle for ordinary layers and enables rotation handles only for rotatable shape layers (`activeLayerSupportsRotation` via `useRect.rotationEnabled`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | `partial` — `src/components/Main/MoveToolArea.tsx:285` |
| Align                      | Six buttons, enabled once two or more layers or groups are selected: Top Edges, Vertical Centers, Bottom Edges, Left Edges, Horizontal Centers and Right Edges. Each moves the selected layers so the named edge or center coincides with the extreme of the selection, or with the selection border. Adobe also states the target as two menu commands — Layer > Align against the selected layers, Layer > Align Layers To Selection against the selection border — and the bar control reaches the same two targets through the `Align to` row below. THIS APP DIVERGES: No align buttons implemented.                                                               | `missing`                                              |
| Distribute                 | The distribute row, enabled only at three or more selected layers: the same six edge and center commands to space the layers evenly between the outermost two, plus the Horizontally and Vertically spacing buttons. The two outermost layers are treated as fixed and only the ones between them move. THIS APP DIVERGES: No distribute buttons implemented.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                              |
| Align to                   | The control that chooses what the align and distribute commands align to: Selection, the default, against the border of the current selection, or Canvas, the whole document. It sits at the right of the alignment group, reached through the three-dot More control, and it changes what the same six buttons do rather than adding a command. Adobe's own account of it is the Canvas route — "To align layers based on the canvas, click the More icon (the three dots) to choose Canvas" — and the Selection default is the state users report as "the alignment is set to 'Selection' and not 'Canvas'". THIS APP DIVERGES: No align target selector implemented. | `missing`                                              |
| Width                      | Numeric text box, in percent, for the layer width. It replaces the Auto-Select controls while a transform is active, and carries a Link icon that is on by default since Photoshop 21.0. THIS APP DIVERGES: No numeric width percentage field in options bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | `missing`                                              |
| Height                     | Numeric text box, in percent, for the layer height, paired with Width through the Link icon so a corner drag scales proportionally. THIS APP DIVERGES: No numeric height percentage field in options bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `missing`                                              |

**Modifiers**

- **Alt** — Drag a duplicate of the layer or selection instead of the original, leaving the source layer where it was. Printed by Adobe as Alt on Windows and Option on macOS. THIS APP DIVERGES: Alt+drag does not duplicate layer; behaves as normal drag.
- **Shift** — Constrain the drag to a single axis, so a sloppy diagonal snaps to purely horizontal or purely vertical movement. THIS APP DIVERGES: Shift does not constrain drag to single axis.
- **Shift** — Click a layer in the canvas or the Layers panel to add it to the current selection rather than replacing it. Adjacent layers need only Shift-click; noncontiguous layers need Ctrl-click (Command-click on macOS). THIS APP DIVERGES: Shift+click does not add layer to selection.
- **Arrow keys** — Nudge the active layer by one pixel when nothing is selected on it, or the selection itself by one pixel when there is. THIS APP DIVERGES: Arrow keys do not nudge layer by 1px (or 10px with Shift).
- **Shift+Arrow keys** — Nudge by ten pixels instead of one. THIS APP DIVERGES: Not implemented.

**Shortcuts**

- `V` — Select the Move tool. Tapping the key selects it; holding it springs the Move tool onto the currently active tool for as long as the key is down, and releasing returns to the tool you were on. Spring-loaded switching is a preference (Preferences > Tools > Spring-loaded Tool Shortcuts) and is on by default.

**In this app:** `partial` — The app moves and resizes through a custom surface, not Photoshop’s Move options-bar controls. Auto-Select: Layer is effectively always on; there is no Group/Layer selector, Show Transform Controls checkbox, alignment/distribution group or align target. The overlay is a resize rectangle for ordinary layers; when the active layer is a rotatable shape, `activeLayerSupportsRotation` enables rotation handles through `useRect.rotationEnabled`. Numeric W/H, reference point and Photoshop’s transform-field bar are absent. Arrow keys nudge the active unlocked non-bedrock layer by one document pixel, or ten with Shift, when no selection is active. Alt-drag duplication, Shift-axis constraint and Shift-click-to-extend are not implemented.

### Free Transform — the Edit > Free Transform command, not a Tools panel Tool

`transform`

Photoshop's Free Transform (Cmd+T) scales, rotates, skews, distorts, adds perspective or warps a layer in one continuous operation.

Free Transform puts a bounding box around the active layer and lets one continuous operation change its size, angle and shape together, which is the point: rotating and rescaling an image in two steps resamples it twice. Every mode is a drag on that box, and the mode is chosen by right-click menu, by an options-bar button, or by holding a modifier so the box changes behavior mid-gesture. Nothing is written to the document until you commit, so a transform can be abandoned and undone as a unit.

**Options bar**

The paired Link icon is on by default since Photoshop 21.0, so a corner handle scales proportionally. THIS APP DIVERGES: Implementation has Resize X slider (10-300%) but NO numeric text field for width percentage. **Modifiers**

- **Shift** — With a rotation drag outside the bounding box, constrain the angle to 15-degree increments. With a handle drag, toggle proportional scaling off and on, which is what Shift means since Photoshop 21.0.
- **Alt** — Distort relative to the center point of the bounding box, so the opposite handle moves at the same time in the opposite direction. Printed by Adobe as Alt on Windows and Option on macOS.
- **Cmd** — Distort freely by dragging a handle, in any direction, with no constraint. Printed by Adobe as Command on macOS and Control on Windows.
- **Cmd+Shift** — Skew: drag a side handle to slant that side while the opposite side stays parallel.
- **Cmd+Alt+Shift** — Perspective: drag a corner handle so the layer recedes toward one edge, the two sides no longer meeting at a right angle.

**Shortcuts**

- `Cmd+T` — Free Transform. Choosing the Move tool and checking Show Transform Controls enters the same state, which is how a pixel layer gets its box.
- `Cmd+Option+T` — Duplicate the layer or selection and enter Free Transform on the duplicate, leaving the original untouched.
- `Enter` — Commit the transform. Selecting another tool or another layer commits it too.

**In this app:** `partial` — Free Transform is a command, not a tool. The primary evidence is a negative one and it is a good one: a complete, version-stamped inventory of the Photoshop 2026 Tools panel lists every entry in the bar — Move, the marquees, the crop, the pen family, the type tools, the shape tools, Hand, Zoom — and has no Transform entry in it, while Photoshop reaches the operation through Edit > Free Transform or Cmd+T. Adobe's own routing agrees, sending a pixel layer to the Move tool with Show Transform Controls rather than to any transform tool. Note the shape of the menu, because it is two items and not one: Edit > Free Transform is a top-level Edit item, and Edit > Transform is a separate submenu carrying the six single modes — Scale, Rotate, Skew, Distort, Perspective and Warp. One counter-sentence exists on Adobe's marketing copy — "Select the Transform tool by pressing Ctrl + T (Cmd + T for Mac)" — but the very next clause of the same page is "You can also go to Edit > Free Transform": the page names the menu route itself, and uses "tool" for the interactive state rather than for a Tools-panel entry. The app reaches the same command from Edit > Free Transform, which is the route Adobe documents, so the route matches and the panel does not: it makes the panel in the options bar a different thing from Free Transform's bar, and the two should not be described as the same control set. Colors and Levels went the other way, out of the toolbar and into Image > Adjustments, because they are commands too; `extraTools` in toolbar-mapping.ts is the list of registered tool ids that deliberately carry no rail entry. What the app builds is a fixed-parameter panel for the Image > Transform operations — rotate 90 degrees left, 180 and 90 degrees right, a continuous rotation slider clamped to plus or minus 90, skew X and skew Y in plus or minus 45 degrees, scale X and Y in 10 to 300 percent, and horizontal and vertical flip — plus one projective operation the app calls Trapezoid (-85 to 85) which is not in Photoshop's Free Transform bar. No numeric text fields for W/H/X/Y/rotation/H/V, no Link icon, no reference point grid, no warp mode switch, no Commit button, Cancel only via Escape. The app's panel is a different control set from Photoshop's Free Transform bar.

### Levels — the Image > Adjustments command, not a Tools panel Tool

`levels`

Photoshop's Levels remaps an image's tonal range through a histogram, a gamma pivot and per-channel black, white and output points.

Levels is the tonal correction tool: it stretches or compresses where the image's darkest and lightest pixels land, and bends the midtones independently of the ends, which is what separates it from a brightness or contrast slider. The histogram above the controls is the working surface — you read where the data actually sits, then move the three input sliders until the blacks reach the black point, the whites the white point, and the middle slider makes the gamma adjustment that sets overall midtone brightness without crushing either end. Every move can be scoped to one color channel, which is how a cast gets removed rather than merely desaturated. The two routes are not equivalent, and Adobe says so: choosing Image > Adjustments > Levels "makes direct adjustments to the image layer and discards image information", while an adjustment layer stays editable.

**Modifiers**

- **Alt** — Hold while dragging the black point or white point slider to see which areas are being clipped, instead of moving the slider. Adobe prints it as Alt on Windows and Option on macOS. Choosing Show Clipping For Black/White Points from the panel menu makes the same preview permanent.

**In this app:** `partial` — FUNDAMENTAL MISMATCH: The app exposes Brightness/Contrast at Image > Adjustments > Brightness/Contrast; its internal tool id is `levels`, but it is NOT Photoshop's Levels command. Photoshop's Levels item is disabled in the app, and the app has no Levels histogram, channel selector, input or output controls, gamma control, Auto command, or eyedroppers. The app's Brightness/Contrast sliders use Adobe's documented ranges: Brightness -150 to +150 and Contrast -50 to +100. The neutral values emit `brightness(100%)` and `contrast(100%)`; the minimum Brightness value emits `brightness(0%)`, which maps normalized channel values to black. The implementation uses CSS `brightness()` and `contrast()` factors. CSS brightness multiplies normalized channel values, and CSS contrast applies a linear adjustment around mid-grey; filter output is clamped to the allowed color range. Factors above 1 can therefore clamp some channel values to black or white. This is the app's CSS mapping, not verified pixel parity with Photoshop: Adobe's current desktop Help page describes the slider ranges and qualitative effects but does not publish the default-mode transfer formula. A committed adjustment is retained as a layer operation and replayed by the renderer, but it is not re-editable; undo is the way to remove it after commit.

### Invert — the Image > Adjustments command, not a Tools panel Tool

`invert`

Photoshop's Invert replaces every channel value with its inverse on the 256-step scale, turning the layer into its negative.

Invert turns an image into its negative: each pixel's brightness in every channel is replaced by its inverse on the 256-step scale, so 255 becomes 0 and 5 becomes 250. It has no dialog and no settings, which is why it is bound to a single chord, Cmd+I. It is used as a creative effect and as a step in building masks, and it is the command that swaps the hidden and revealed areas of a selected layer mask. Chosen from Image > Adjustments it changes the layer's pixels directly; the non-destructive route is an Invert adjustment layer. With an active selection it inverts only the selected pixels.

_Photoshop gives this tool no options bar of its own._

**Shortcuts**

- `Cmd+I` — Apply Invert to the active layer, or to the selected pixels when a selection is active.

**In this app:** `implemented` — Invert is a one-shot command here as in Photoshop: Image > Adjustments > Invert and Cmd+I both call the same command, which commits one raster history state and never becomes the current tool, so it has no options bar and no rail tile. Alpha is left as it is; only the colour channels are inverted. An active selection clips the inversion, and a feathered or anti-aliased edge blends each pixel toward its inverse by its selection coverage rather than stepping. Two differences from Photoshop are deliberate. First, the command refuses the bedrock layer, which is the document's backing image and which no raster edit in this app targets; Photoshop inverts its Background layer. Second, there are no adjustment layers and no layer masks, so the Invert adjustment layer and inverting a selected mask have nothing to act on. While another tool's live preview (Levels, Color, Free Transform) is still uncommitted on the layer, Invert does nothing rather than discard that preview; switching tools commits it.
